f0.summary: A young republic of farms, ports and restless settlers, looking west across the Mississippi.
history: Sixty years after its independence, the United States stretches from the Atlantic seaboard to the Louisiana Purchase. Andrew Jackson is in the last year of his presidency; his war on the Bank of the United States and his removal of the southeastern nations beyond the Mississippi have divided the country, and Arkansas and Michigan are about to join the Union.

Americans have been settling in Mexican Texas for fifteen years, and many in the southern states openly hope the rebellion there will end in annexation. In the northwest the republic shares the Oregon Country with Britain under the joint occupation agreed in 1818, and its fur men already work the passes of the Rockies.

The regular army is small, a few thousand men scattered along the frontier forts, but the states can raise militia in numbers no neighbour can match. The navy keeps squadrons in the Atlantic, the Caribbean and the Pacific.

traits.name: Westward Settlers
traits.effect: Land units pay 15% less movement in forests.

f1.summary: The largest state of the Americas, rich in silver and divided over who should rule it.
history: Mexico won its independence from Spain in 1821 and reaches from Yucatán to the Pacific coast of Alta California. Its governments have risen and fallen by pronunciamiento ever since. In 1835 General Antonio López de Santa Anna set aside the federal constitution of 1824, and several states rose against the new centralist order.

Texas was one of them. Santa Anna marched north to crush the rebels, took the Alamo in March 1836 and was then routed and captured at San Jacinto. In Mexico City the acting president, José Justo Corro, and congress refuse to recognise the treaties the captive general signed, and insist that Texas is still Mexican.

The silver mines of Zacatecas and Guanajuato pay for a large army of regulars and active militia, but the treasury is always short, the northern frontier is thinly held, and Yucatán and the far north resent rule from the capital.

f2.summary: A rebel republic of a few thousand settlers, declared in March 1836 and fighting for its life.
history: Americans came to Mexican Texas from the 1820s at the invitation of empresarios such as Stephen F. Austin, and by 1835 they far outnumbered the Tejano population. When Santa Anna abolished the federal constitution, the colonists rose, drove the Mexican garrisons out of San Antonio, and on 2 March 1836 declared independence at Washington-on-the-Brazos.

The Alamo fell four days later and the prisoners taken at Goliad were shot. Sam Houston's small army retreated east, drawing the Mexican columns after it, until it turned and routed Santa Anna at San Jacinto on 21 April. The republic survives, but its treasury is empty and its army is made of volunteers who may go home.

Texas can call on the Rangers, mounted frontier volunteers, and on sympathisers across the Sabine in the United States. It holds little beyond the settled river valleys between the Sabine and the Nueces.

traits.name: Remember the Alamo
traits.effect: Units defend 15% better in the republic's own provinces.

f3.government: Crown colonies and the Hudson's Bay Company
f3.summary: Britain's American colonies and the fur empire of the Hudson's Bay Company, held by the Royal Navy.
history: Britain took New France in 1763 and kept its northern colonies when the thirteen to the south broke away. Upper and Lower Canada, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland are governed from London through appointed governors; the Earl of Gosford, at Quebec, is trying to calm an assembly that is close to revolt.

West and north of the Canadas lies Rupert's Land, the vast drainage of Hudson Bay, ruled as a trading monopoly by the Hudson's Bay Company from York Factory. Its brigades reach the Pacific, where the Company shares the Oregon Country with the Americans. In this scenario the Russian-American coast to the northwest is counted within its reach.

Britain's strength here is the Royal Navy. It holds Jamaica, the Bahamas, Trinidad, Guiana and, since 1833, the Falkland Islands, and no fleet in the Americas can face it. The garrisons ashore are small and the distances immense.

f4.summary: The heart of Bolívar's old Gran Colombia, from the isthmus of Panama to the Andes of Quito.
history: Simón Bolívar's Gran Colombia joined New Granada, Venezuela and Ecuador in the wars of independence, and fell apart in 1830, the year he died. The Republic of New Granada was proclaimed in 1831, and Francisco de Paula Santander, once Bolívar's vice-president and later his rival, returned from exile to become its president in 1832.

Venezuela, dominated by José Antonio Páez, and Ecuador under Vicente Rocafuerte went their own way, but the three republics share an army tradition, a border with the new confederation in the south and a fear of its ambitions. In this scenario they stand together under New Granada.

The republic spans the isthmus of Panama, the Caribbean coast, the valleys of the Magdalena and the cordilleras. Its roads are mule tracks over the mountains, which makes it hard to rule and harder still to invade.

f5.ruler: Supreme Protector Andrés de Santa Cruz
f5.government: Confederation of three states under a protector
f5.summary: Andrés de Santa Cruz's bid to reunite Peru and Bolivia, won by conquest in 1835 and 1836.
history: Peru and Upper Peru had been one viceroyalty under Spain. Andrés de Santa Cruz, president of Bolivia since 1829, was invited into Peru's civil war in 1835 and won it: he defeated Agustín Gamarra at Yanacocha and Felipe Santiago Salaverry at Socabaya, and had Salaverry shot in February 1836.

Santa Cruz divided Peru into North and South Peru and joined them with Bolivia in a confederation under himself as Supreme Protector, confirmed at Tacna in 1837. The silver of Potosí and the ports of the Pacific coast are his, and so is the enmity of Chile and the Argentine Confederation, who see a new great power on their borders.
His army is the best-drilled in South America, built around Bolivian veterans such as the Colorados regiment. It is not large, and it must hold the whole length of the Andes.

traits.name: Royal Road
traits.effect: Land units pay 15% less movement in mountains.

f6.ruler: Emperor Pedro II, under the Regent Diogo Antônio Feijó
f6.summary: The only monarchy in the Americas, vast and rich, ruled by regents for a ten-year-old emperor.
history: Brazil became an empire in 1822, when the Portuguese prince Pedro declared its independence rather than return to Lisbon. He abdicated in 1831 in favour of his five-year-old son, and the empire has been governed by regents ever since; Father Diogo Antônio Feijó has held the office since 1835.

The regency is beset by provincial revolts. The Cabanagem has held Belém and much of Pará since 1835, and in Rio Grande do Sul the Ragamuffin rebels proclaimed a republic in 1836. Sugar and a rising trade in coffee make the empire rich, and the slave trade, outlawed on paper, goes on.
Brazil keeps the strongest navy in South America and an army that must reach from the Amazon to the River Plate, most of it along rivers rather than roads.

traits.name: River Fleets
traits.effect: Land units pay 20% less movement in forests.

f7.government: Confederation of provinces, led by Buenos Aires
f7.summary: The provinces of the River Plate under Rosas, allied here with Chile against Santa Cruz.
history: The provinces of the old viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata declared independence in 1816 and then fought each other for twenty years. The Federal Pact of 1831 bound them into a loose confederation, and in 1835 Buenos Aires gave its governor, Juan Manuel de Rosas, the sum of public power. Rosas conducts the confederation's foreign affairs and rules through the gauchos and the mazorca.

Across the Andes, Chile's minister Diego Portales has built a strong conservative state and regards Santa Cruz's confederation as a threat to its existence; Chile declares war on it in 1836, and Rosas follows in 1837. In this scenario Chile and the Argentine provinces fight as one.

The confederation's strength is its cavalry: gauchos of the pampas, and the Colorados del Monte raised on Rosas' own estates. Beyond the frontier forts, Patagonia belongs to the Tehuelche and the Mapuche.

traits.name: Open Pampas
traits.effect: Land units pay 10% less movement on plains.
